cause: Mouthpiece too far out on the cork
evidence: All notes flat by a similar amount (cents offset roughly uniform across both registers); tone otherwise normal.
advice: Push the mouthpiece further onto the cork — about 1 mm per 2-3 cents flat (more in the upper register). Re-check with a tuner on G4 and C6.
why: The mouthpiece position changes the length of the whole air column: every note moves together. Pushing in 1 mm raises pitch by ~1.4 cents on low Bb and ~3.3 cents on C#5.
listen_for: With a drone or tuner the whole instrument sits low, low notes and high notes alike.

cause: Mouthpiece too far in on the cork
evidence: All notes sharp by a similar amount.
advice: Pull the mouthpiece out a little — about 1 mm per 2-3 cents sharp. Do not 'lip down' to compensate.
why: A shorter air column raises every note by roughly the same proportion.
listen_for: Everything sits high on the tuner, and relaxing the lip does not fix the low notes.

cause: Biting / too much lip pressure
evidence: Upper register and palm-key notes increasingly sharp, a thinner, pinched sound; ff does not open up.
advice: Relax the jaw and let the lower lip cushion the reed instead of pushing it; think 'drop the jaw, keep the corners firm'. Re-tune after relaxing.
why: Lip force pre-bends the reed toward the lay: the reed becomes stiffer (the lip tissue stiffens as you press) and its opening smaller, which raises pitch most on short tubes and limits the flow.
listen_for: Pitch rising as you go up the horn, high notes thin and 'tight'; when you relax, the pitch drops and the sound gets bigger.

cause: Embouchure too loose (not enough lip support)
evidence: Upper notes flat and spread; low notes may honk; pitch unstable.
advice: Firm the lip a little (corners in, chin flat) so the reed is supported; keep the air steady.
why: Too little lip force leaves the reed very compliant and wide open: the reed's 'equivalent volume' grows, lowering high notes most.
listen_for: High notes sagging flat and wide, the sound spreading at forte.

cause: Too much mouthpiece in the mouth
evidence: Notes flat (more in the upper register), loud and spread; low notes may crack to the octave.
advice: Take a little less mouthpiece: place the lower lip about where the reed starts to leave the mouthpiece rail (mark it with a pencil line).
why: The lip sits further from the reed tip, so the free vibrating reed is longer and softer: more reed compliance, lower pitch, less control.
listen_for: A big but uncontrolled sound, flat and wobbly high notes.

cause: Too little mouthpiece in the mouth
evidence: Small, stuffy sound, low notes hard to start; slightly sharp.
advice: Take a little more mouthpiece (a few millimetres) so the reed can vibrate freely.
why: A short free reed is stiff: higher closing pressure, less flow, a smaller and darker sound.
listen_for: Low notes refusing to speak softly, a pinched small tone.
gaps: In the simulator, moving the lip toward the tip raises the reed's closing pressure, the opposite of some real set-ups — treat as a hint.

cause: Heavy lip cushion / damping (subtone-like)
evidence: Dark, soft-edged sound with little 2-5 kHz energy at every dynamic; slightly flat.
advice: Use a little less lower lip over the reed and less pressure from the lip tissue; let the reed ring.
why: Lip tissue on the reed absorbs its vibration (damping), which removes upper partials and lowers the effective reed resonance.
listen_for: A muffled tone that stays dark even when you play louder.

cause: Too little lip cushion (thin lip, 'reed buzz')
evidence: Edgy/buzzy tone with strong 2-5 kHz energy, especially loud.
advice: Roll a little more of the lower lip over the teeth to cushion the reed.
why: With little damping the reed's own resonance rings, adding high-frequency buzz.
listen_for: A 'zzz' edge on every note.

cause: Reed too hard for the set-up
evidence: Stuffy, needs a lot of air; soft notes hard to start; dark; slightly sharp.
advice: Try half a strength softer (or sand the reed slightly) and compare the low notes at pp.
why: A stiffer reed raises the closing pressure, so more blowing pressure is needed before the reed sounds.
listen_for: Effort and resistance; low notes cracking or not speaking softly.

cause: Reed too soft
evidence: Upper register flat, sound closes up or buzzes at ff, bright and thin.
advice: Try half a strength harder.
why: A soft reed closes easily: the pitch of high notes sags and loud notes choke.
listen_for: High notes going flat as you crescendo; the sound 'shutting off' when you push.

cause: Wide tip opening (jazz set-up) without the matching embouchure
evidence: Loud and bright, wide intonation, low notes cracking; more air needed.
advice: Either a closer facing / softer reed, or more lip support; check G4 pp holds pitch.
why: A larger reed opening lets more air through: louder and brighter, but the reed is harder to control.
listen_for: Big sound but unstable pitch, hard to play softly.

cause: Bright mouthpiece (high baffle / small chamber)
evidence: Bright, edgy tone across the range, more so than the embouchure explains; register 2 slightly sharp.
advice: If you want a darker/classical sound: a lower-baffle, larger-chamber mouthpiece. Otherwise it is a style choice.
why: A high baffle narrows the air path just behind the tip, which boosts upper partials.
listen_for: A bright 'cutting' tone even at mf.
gaps: Baffle and chamber are partly confounded with each other in this test set (|corr| ≈ 0.65-0.73).

cause: Large-chamber (dark) mouthpiece
evidence: Dark tone; the upper register flat relative to the low register (octaves narrow).
advice: Adjust with the cork for the middle of the horn, then voice the upper register up (tongue higher) — or use a smaller-chamber mouthpiece for better octaves.
why: A larger mouthpiece volume replaces the cut-off tip of the cone less well at high frequencies: the second register goes flat relative to the first.
listen_for: Octaves (G4–G5, D4–D5) that are narrow (top note flat).

cause: Not enough air support
evidence: Soft, thin sound at mf, little brightening from pp to ff, notes slow to start.
advice: Breathe lower and keep a steady, faster air stream; practise long tones crescendo pp→ff.
why: Blowing pressure sets how far above the oscillation threshold the reed works: too little gives a weak, unstable note.
listen_for: Notes that fade or wobble at the end of a phrase; small dynamic range.

cause: Over-blowing (too much pressure for the set-up)
evidence: Loud and harsh at mf, low notes jumping up an octave, slight pitch drop.
advice: Use less pressure and more air speed control; let the reed do the work.
why: At high pressure the reed beats hard against the lay: a harsh spectrum and register jumps on the low notes.
listen_for: Low Bb/C cracking to the octave, an edgy forte that you cannot soften.

cause: Closed throat / jaw in the low register
evidence: Low notes slightly sharp and pinched compared with the middle register.
advice: Open the throat and drop the jaw for the low notes ('aw' or 'oh' vowel).
why: The mouth cavity is in series with the horn at the reed; a smaller cavity slightly raises the pitch and thins the low notes.
listen_for: Low notes thinner and higher than the middle register.
gaps: Weakly identifiable from the test set (the tract mainly matters in the upper register).

cause: Low notes cracking to the octave (air/lip balance)
evidence: regime ≠ 1 on Bb3 or D4 (sounds an octave or twelfth up).
advice: Less pressure and a slightly looser lip for the low notes, more mouth cavity ('aw'); start them softly with a gentle tongue.
why: For the lowest notes the 2nd air-column resonance is as strong as the 1st; too much pressure or lip force tips the reed into the upper regime.
listen_for: The note popping up an octave as you push.

cause: Unstable / sharp open C#5
evidence: C#5 sharp by > 15 cents or pitch_std high relative to C5.
advice: Relax the lip and voice lower on C#5; try adding the low C# key or RH fingers (standard alternate) to stabilise it.
why: Open C# vents through a small hole with a very short tube: its resonances are weak and inharmonic.
listen_for: A thin, wavering C#5.

cause: Voicing set late (scooping into notes)
evidence: Large |scoop| (> 25 cents) at the start of notes, mostly on palm-key / upper notes.
advice: Set the tongue/throat shape before you start the note ('voice, then attack'), then release the tongue.
why: The vocal tract is in series with the horn; if its shape changes during the attack the pitch slides.
listen_for: A pitch 'swoop' at the start of high notes.
gaps: Attack/scoop features are unreliable in reverberant recordings; only trust with a close, dry recording.

cause: Breathy / air leaking
evidence: Low harmonic-to-noise ratio (hnr) on most notes relative to the other notes.
advice: Seal the corners of the mouth around the mouthpiece; keep the air focused; check the reed for leaks.
why: Air that does not pass the reed channel as a modulated jet adds broadband noise.
listen_for: A 'hiss' under the tone.

cause: Small dynamic range (pp too loud or ff too weak)
evidence: G4 ff − pp level < 5 dB (the default simulated player gives ~7 dB on this protocol; real players typically 15-25 dB), little brightening.
advice: For pp: more lip support and less mouthpiece pressure-air (firmer, smaller opening); for ff: more air with a looser, undamped lip.
why: Dynamics on a reed instrument come mainly from the embouchure: the lip sets the reed's closing pressure, which scales the whole oscillation; pressure alone only changes the level by ~6-12 dB.
listen_for: pp and ff sounding almost the same.
gaps: The simulator's pp intonation in register 2 is up to +40-60 cents sharp (A5, Bb5) — pp pitch advice is suppressed there.

cause: Pinching at soft dynamics
evidence: The pp note is more than 15 cents sharper than the same note at mf.
advice: For soft notes keep the jaw relaxed and support the sound with air and lip corners rather than biting; drop the jaw slightly as you get softer.
why: Playing softly with a firmer lip reduces the reed opening and stiffens the reed (strain-stiffening lip tissue): the pitch rises, most in the upper register.
listen_for: Soft notes drifting sharp on a tuner, especially G5–C6.
gaps: The simulator's pp intonation in register 2 runs +40-60 cents sharp on A5/Bb5 — G4 is used for this check.
